posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging on a compliance/explainability pain point — validate the 'black box' problem from an operator's perspective, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is basically the end of the conversation in any regulated environment. What's interesting is it's not really a trust gap with AI — it's a trust gap with outputs that have no audit trail attached to them. Numbers without lineage aren't analytics, they're just confident-sounding guesses. Curious whether you think this is fixable at the tool level or whether it's more of a process and governance problem?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the trust gap as the real problem, not the tooling
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the hard part. It's that finance teams have been burned before — a number was wrong once, someone got embarrassed in front of the board, and now Excel feels safer because at least they know where the bodies are buried. 18 months of build doesn't fix 18 months of that kind of history. What did the moment of distrust actually look like for your team?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add depth on why usage is the real signal, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a confession that nobody could agree on what mattered, so they kept everything. The jump from 10% to 85% usage is the real stat here — that's not a BI win, that's an org alignment win that happened to show up in the tooling. Most teams never make that cut because deleting a metric feels like telling someone their work doesn't matter. What finally gave your team the cover to drop the other 42?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that tooling isn't the problem, governance is, without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone blames the tool but the tool just made the underlying problem visible faster — there was never one definition of revenue, it just lived in one person's head before. Self-service BI doesn't create the chaos, it just democratises it. So the real question is: who had the authority to define 'truth' before, and why don't they have it now?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as security risk with CEO prospect engaged — validate the reframe, add the trust accountability layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The security framing is the right one and I don't think enough people are saying it yet. A hallucinated number in a dashboard isn't just wrong — it's an unaudited input that shaped a real decision, and nobody signed off on it. We obsess over who accessed the data, but almost never over whether the AI's interpretation of it was trustworthy in the first place. Who in your org is actually accountable when that chain breaks?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the core pain with a specific observation, add the insight that the problem is design philosophy not complexity
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number is almost irrelevant — we've seen the same thing happen with tools that cost a tenth of that. The real issue is that most platforms are built to impress a data team in a demo, not to answer a question for a ops manager on a Tuesday morning. Vendors call it self-service but what they mean is 'you can do it yourself if you know SQL.' What would it actually look like if the business user — not the builder — was the one the tool was designed around?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely ICP company has surfaced a classic data trust problem — validate the culture diagnosis but add the layer about why tools rarely help people see where the disagreement is actually happening
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three different answers — that's not a data problem, that's a 'nobody agreed on what the question meant' problem. Culture gets the blame but honestly the tools don't help either, most dashboards just show the number, not the assumptions baked into it. Makes the CFO conversation brutal because there's nothing to point at. Does anyone in those three teams even know where the filters diverge?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing adoption and shadow AI pain in a Microsoft Copilot thread — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' root cause and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me — most rollouts skip the harder question of whether people actually understand their own workflows well enough to prompt anything useful. Shadow AI is just people solving that gap themselves, which is honestly kind of rational. The tool being 'locked down' is usually just cover for 'the outputs don't match how I actually think about my job.' What does the 12% have in common — are they heavy Excel users or something else?
